chapter_note.about: A tree is a set of nodes joined by edges, with one root on top and children below. This chapter covers the vocabulary and height, node-count identities, the three depth-first traversals, rebuilding a tree from traversals, binary search trees with search, insertion and deletion, how insertion order shapes a BST, counting trees, AVL balancing, the array form of a complete tree, operation costs, and recursion on trees in C and Python. It is the heaviest data-structure chapter in GATE, because one idea, a recursive definition (a root with a left tree and a right tree), explains almost every question.
chapter_note.simple: A tree is a family tree turned upside down: one ancestor at the top, children below, and people with no children at the bottom. To list everyone you walk round the tree, left side before right, and choose whether to write a person's name before, between or after their two sides. A search tree keeps smaller names on the left and bigger on the right, so finding someone is a game of higher or lower. If names are added in alphabetical order the tree becomes a long stick and the game gets slow. Balanced versions twist a few links to keep the tree short. Almost every tree question is solved by asking: what does the root do, and what do the left and right trees give back?

cards.title: Terms and height
cards.simple: Think of a family tree turned upside down. The oldest ancestor is at the top (the root), each person has children below, and people with no children are at the bottom (leaves). How many steps down you are from the root is your depth. The longest chain of steps from the top to the bottom is the height of the tree. In exam words: root, parent, child, leaf, internal node; depth is edges from the root; height is edges on the longest root-to-leaf path, so a single node has height 0.
cards.idea: A tree is a set of nodes joined by edges, with one special node on top called the **root**. Each node can have **children**; a node with no children is a **leaf**, and every other node is **internal**. The **depth** of a node counts edges from the root. The **height** of the tree counts edges on the longest path from the root down to a leaf.
cards.definition:
For a tree with root `r`:

- **Parent / child:** the node above / below along an edge.
- **Leaf:** a node with no children. **Internal node:** a node with at least one child.
- **Depth** of a node: the number of edges from `r` to it (`r` has depth 0).
- **Height** of the tree: the maximum depth of any node, counted in edges. A single node has height 0, and the empty tree has height -1.
- A binary tree has at most two children per node (left and right).
cards.intuition_full: These words are about direction and counting. Depth looks upward from a node to the root; height looks downward from the root to the deepest leaf. Both count edges, the arrows between nodes, and not nodes. That is why a lone root has height 0: there is no edge to cross. Counting edges also makes recursion neat. The height of a tree is 1 + the larger height of its two subtrees, and the empty subtree gets -1 so that a leaf comes out as 1 + max(-1, -1) = 0. Many exam questions turn on a single convention: 'height' in edges versus 'levels' or 'height' in nodes. Always read the definition in the question. A good check is to draw the longest path, count its edges and its nodes, and see which number the question asks for.

examples.setup: Look at this tree: A is the root with children B and C. B has children D and E. E has one child, G. C has one child, F. Find the depth of G, the number of leaves, the number of internal nodes, and the height.
steps: A is the root. Its children are B and C. B has children D and E, E has the child G, and C has the child F.
Depth is the number of edges from the root. A is 0. B and C are 1. D, E and F are 2. G is 3.
Leaves have no children: D, G and F. That is 3 leaves.
Internal nodes have at least one child: A, B, C and E. That is 4 internal nodes, and 4 + 3 = 7 nodes in all.
Height is the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. A, B, E, G has 3 edges (4 nodes). So the height is 3, not 4.
examples.answer: G has depth 3, there are 3 leaves and 4 internal nodes, and the height is 3 (counting edges). The same path has 4 nodes, which is why the convention matters.

examples.setup: A binary tree has 20 nodes. What are the smallest and largest possible heights, counting edges?
steps: Largest height: a chain, where each node has one child. 20 nodes in a line have 19 edges, so height 19.
Smallest height: pack the nodes as tightly as possible. A binary tree of height h holds at most 2^(h+1) - 1 nodes.
h = 3 holds at most 15 nodes: too few for 20. h = 4 holds at most 31: enough.
So the smallest height is 4 (that is floor(log2 20) = 4).
examples.answer: Smallest 4, largest 19. Height ranges from floor(log2 n) up to n - 1 for n nodes.

examples.setup: State the height (in edges) of: an empty tree, a tree with a single node, and a tree whose longest root-to-leaf path has 6 nodes.
steps: A single node has no edges on its longest path: height 0.
The path with 6 nodes has 5 edges between them: height 5.
The empty tree has no node at all. By the usual convention that makes a single node 0, the empty tree is -1.
That -1 is why recursive height code returns -1 for NULL and why 1 + max(left, right) gives 0 for a leaf.
examples.answer: Empty -1, single node 0, six-node path 5. Check whether the question counts height in edges or in levels before computing.

cards.title: Node-count identities
cards.simple: Picture a company where every manager has exactly two people reporting to them, or none. Start with one person, who is both boss and a leaf. Each time someone gets two new reports, one leaf disappears and two appear, so the leaves go up by one, and so does the number of managers. That is why there is always exactly one more leaf than manager. In exam words: in a full binary tree, leaves = internal nodes + 1, and a binary tree of height h has at most 2^(h+1) - 1 nodes.
cards.idea: Counting nodes in a tree follows simple identities. In a **full** binary tree, the number of leaves is always one more than the number of internal nodes. In a general binary tree, the same relation holds for the nodes with two children. A height limit caps the number of nodes: a tree of height `h` has at most `2^(h+1) - 1`.
cards.definition:
Let `n0`, `n1`, `n2` be the numbers of nodes with 0, 1, 2 children in a binary tree, and `N` the total.

- `N = n0 + n1 + n2` and the number of edges is `N - 1 = n1 + 2 x n2`.
- So `n0 = n2 + 1`. For a full binary tree (`n1 = 0`): `L = I + 1` and `N = 2L - 1`.
- A full `k`-ary tree: `L = (k - 1) x I + 1`.
- Binary tree of height `h`: at most `2^(h+1) - 1` nodes and `2^h` leaves.
cards.intuition_full: Everything here is edge counting. A tree with N nodes always has N - 1 edges, since each non-root node has exactly one edge to its parent. The same edges can also be counted from the top: every node contributes as many edges as it has children. Setting the two counts equal gives the leaf relation. The picture of growing a full tree helps you remember it. You begin with one leaf. Each growth step replaces a leaf by an internal node with two leaves, so internal nodes go up by one and leaves go up by one. The upper bound on nodes for height h comes from filling every level: 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^h = 2^(h+1) - 1. The bound is reached exactly by the perfect tree. For k-ary trees replace 2 by k in the same arguments.

examples.setup: A full binary tree (every node has 0 or 2 children) has 6 leaves. How many internal nodes and how many nodes in total does it have?
steps: The tree shown is full: every node has 0 or 2 children. It has 6 leaves.
Start from a single node: 1 leaf and 0 internal nodes. Give a leaf two children: that node becomes internal (+1 internal), one leaf is lost and two are gained (+1 leaf net).
So after every such step, leaves = internal + 1. With 6 leaves there are 5 internal nodes.
Total nodes = leaves + internal = 6 + 5 = 11, which is also 2 x 6 - 1.
examples.answer: 5 internal nodes and 11 nodes in total. In a full binary tree, leaves = internal nodes + 1.

examples.setup: Every internal node of a tree has exactly 4 children. The tree has 10 internal nodes and 31 leaves. Check this is consistent and find the total number of nodes. In general, how many leaves does a full k-ary tree with I internal nodes have?
steps: Count the edges two ways. Each internal node has k children, so there are k x I edges.
A tree with N nodes has N - 1 edges. N = I + L (internal plus leaves). So k x I = I + L - 1.
Solve for L: L = (k - 1) x I + 1. For k = 4 and I = 10: L = 3 x 10 + 1 = 31. It matches.
Total = I + L = 10 + 31 = 41 nodes.
examples.answer: Consistent: 41 nodes. The general rule is L = (k - 1) x I + 1; for k = 2 it is the familiar L = I + 1.

examples.setup: A binary tree (nodes may have 0, 1 or 2 children) has 8 leaves. Is the total number of nodes determined?
steps: Let n0, n1, n2 be the numbers of nodes with 0, 1 and 2 children. Edges: n1 + 2 x n2 = (n0 + n1 + n2) - 1.
That simplifies to n0 = n2 + 1. With n0 = 8, n2 = 7.
The nodes with one child, n1, are not constrained at all.
Total = 8 + 7 + n1 = 15 + n1, so any value from 15 upward is possible.
examples.answer: No. The number of nodes with two children is determined (7), but one-child nodes are free, so the total is 15 or more.

cards.title: Traversals
cards.simple: A traversal is a way of walking round a tree and writing down every node once. The walk always handles the left side before the right side. The only choice is when to write the node's own name: before visiting its sides (preorder), between them (inorder), or after both (postorder). It is like reading a book's chapters: you can read the chapter title before its sections, in the middle of them, or after them. In exam words: preorder is node-left-right, inorder is left-node-right, postorder is left-right-node.
cards.idea: A **traversal** visits every node exactly once in a fixed order. Depth-first traversals are defined recursively on the three parts: the node `N`, the left subtree `L` and the right subtree `R`, with `L` always before `R`. There is also **level order**, which goes row by row using a queue.
cards.definition:
For a tree with root `N`, left subtree `L`, right subtree `R`:

- **Preorder:** visit `N`, then preorder of `L`, then preorder of `R`.
- **Inorder:** inorder of `L`, then `N`, then inorder of `R`.
- **Postorder:** postorder of `L`, then postorder of `R`, then `N`.
- **Level order:** row by row, left to right (a queue).

On an expression tree, preorder gives prefix and postorder gives postfix.
cards.intuition_full: Each rule is a three-step recipe applied at every node. Write N, L and R on a scrap and replace each letter by the recipe for its subtree, working down until you reach NULL (which contributes nothing). The root is the first item of the preorder, the last item of the postorder, and has the whole left subtree before it in the inorder. That position fact is the key to the next card, rebuilding trees. Expression trees show why the orders matter: a postorder walk visits operands first, then the operator, which is exactly the order a stack evaluates postfix. Inorder prints the usual infix reading but loses brackets. Level order uses a queue because it must finish a whole row before the next one, which is a breadth-first idea, not a recursive one.

examples.setup: Write the preorder, inorder and postorder of this tree. P is the root. P's left child is Q (children S and T). P's right child is R, whose left child is U and whose right child is V. V has a right child W and no left child.
steps: The tree: P at the top, Q (with S, T) on the left, R (with U, V) on the right, W below V on the right. The three orders differ only in when the node is written relative to its subtrees.
Preorder (node, left, right): write P first, then the whole left subtree in preorder: Q S T.
Then the right subtree in preorder: R U V W. Preorder = P Q S T R U V W.
Inorder (left, node, right): the whole left subtree first, in inorder: S Q T.
Then P, then the right subtree in inorder: U R V W. Inorder = S Q T P U R V W.
Postorder (left, right, node): the left subtree first, in postorder: S T Q.
Then the right subtree in postorder: U W V R, and the root P last. Postorder = S T Q U W V R P.
examples.answer: Preorder P Q S T R U V W, inorder S Q T P U R V W, postorder S T Q U W V R P. The root is first, in the middle, and last.

examples.setup: An expression tree has root `*`. Its left child is `-` with leaves 7 and 3. Its right child is `+` with leaves 2 and 4. Write the postfix and prefix forms, evaluate the tree, and say what its inorder reading gives.
steps: Postorder (left, right, node) gives postfix: 7 3 - 2 4 + *.
Preorder (node, left, right) gives prefix: * - 7 3 + 2 4.
Evaluate: 7 - 3 = 4 and 2 + 4 = 6, then 4 x 6 = 24.
Inorder reading: 7 - 3 * 2 + 4. It has lost the brackets, so as a plain expression it would mean 7 - (3 x 2) + 4 = 5, not 24.
examples.answer: Postfix `7 3 - 2 4 + *` with value 24; the prefix form is in step 2. Plain inorder drops the brackets, so it is ambiguous without them.

examples.setup: A tree has 4 nodes in a chain: A is the root, B is the left child of A, C is the left child of B, D is the left child of C. Write its three traversals.
steps: Preorder: A, then its only subtree: B, C, D. So A B C D.
Inorder (left, node, right): the left subtree comes first, then the node. D C B A.
Postorder (left, right, node): the left subtree first, then the node. D C B A.
In a left-leaning chain, inorder and postorder are the same.
examples.answer: Preorder A B C D; inorder D C B A; postorder D C B A. Two different traversals can coincide on a skewed tree, so do not assume they always differ.

cards.why: Traversals are the most-tested tree topic. In GATE: write one traversal from a given tree, find the position of a node, or recognise a definition (2021 CS2 Q26, 2026 CS2 Q12, 2023 CS Q47, 2016 CS2 Q36).
how: Recipe: preorder N L R, inorder L N R, postorder L R N.
Work recursively: expand each subtree with the same recipe.
Write the nodes in a line as you visit them; never skip NULL children silently.
Check: the root is first (pre), last (post) or has its left subtree before it (in).
cards.mistake: Reading postorder or preorder left to right on the picture instead of following the recipe. For postorder the root comes last, not first; for inorder the root sits between the left and right subtrees. Following the recipe on a skewed tree is also safer than trusting the shape.
edge_cases: Empty tree: all traversals are empty.
Single node: all three equal.
Left-skewed chain: inorder equals postorder.
Right-skewed chain: preorder equals inorder.

cards.what: A **traversal** visits every node exactly once in a fixed order. Depth-first traversals are defined recursively on the three parts: the node `N`, the left subtree `L` and the right subtree `R`, with `L` always before `R`. cards.what_full:

For a tree with root `N`, left subtree `L`, right subtree `R`:

- **Preorder:** visit `N`, then preorder of `L`, then preorder of `R`.
- **Inorder:** inorder of `L`, then `N`, then inorder of `R`.
- **Postorder:** postorder of `L`, then postorder of `R`, then `N`.
- **Level order:** row by row, left to right (a queue).

On an expression tree, preorder gives prefix and postorder gives postfix.

**Worked example.** Write the preorder, inorder and postorder of this tree. P is the root. P's left child is Q (children S and T). P's right child is R, whose left child is U and whose right child is V. V has a right child W and no left child.

1. The tree: P at the top, Q (with S, T) on the left, R (with U, V) on the right, W below V on the right. The three orders differ only in when the node is written relative to its subtrees.
2. Preorder (node, left, right): write P first, then the whole left subtree in preorder: Q S T.
3. Then the right subtree in preorder: R U V W. Preorder = P Q S T R U V W.
4. Inorder (left, node, right): the whole left subtree first, in inorder: S Q T.
5. Then P, then the right subtree in inorder: U R V W. Inorder = S Q T P U R V W.
6. Postorder (left, right, node): the left subtree first, in postorder: S T Q.
7. Then the right subtree in postorder: U W V R, and the root P last. Postorder = S T Q U W V R P.

**Answer:** Preorder P Q S T R U V W, inorder S Q T P U R V W, postorder S T Q U W V R P. The root is first, in the middle, and last.

cards.title: Rebuild from traversals
cards.simple: Imagine two clues about a family photo. One list says in what order people were introduced, which always begins with the boss. The other says who stands where from left to right. Find the boss in the left-to-right list: everyone on the left of the boss is in the left group, and everyone on the right is in the right group. Then repeat inside each group. cards.idea: A single traversal does not fix a tree, but two can. With **inorder** and either **preorder** or **postorder**, the tree is unique. The root comes from the preorder (first item) or the postorder (last item). The inorder tells you which nodes lie in the left subtree and which in the right.
cards.definition:
To rebuild from `pre` and `in`:

1. `root = pre[0]`. Find it in `in` at position `i`.
2. Left subtree: `in[0..i-1]`, with the next `i` items of `pre`.
3. Right subtree: `in[i+1..]`, with the rest of `pre`.
4. Recurse on both parts.

From `post` and `in`: the root is `post[-1]`; the left part takes the first `i` items of `post`. Preorder with postorder works only for **full** binary trees.
cards.intuition_full: The root has a special position in each list: first in preorder, last in postorder, and in the inorder it separates its left subtree from its right. That single fact splits the problem into two smaller ones of known size. The size of the left part tells you how many items of the preorder (or postorder) belong to it, because preorder lists a whole left subtree before the right one. Inorder is essential: given only pre and post, a node with one child could hang on either side, as in the twist example. Full binary trees avoid that, since a node's two children are both present, so the first item after the root in preorder is the left child's subtree and the preorder-postorder boundary can be located.

examples.setup: A binary tree has preorder K C A E R M T and inorder A C E K M R T. Rebuild the tree and write its postorder.
steps: The first item of the preorder is the root: K. Find K in the inorder: A C E | K | M R T. So the left subtree has 3 nodes (A, C, E) and the right subtree has 3 (M, R, T).
Left subtree: its preorder is the next 3 items, C A E. The first, C, is its root. In the inorder A C E, C splits A | C | E.
A and E are alone on each side of C, so they are C's left and right children (leaves).
Right subtree: its preorder is R M T. The root is R. In the inorder M R T it splits M | R | T, so M and T are leaves.
The tree is K(C(A, E), R(M, T)). Postorder (left, right, node): A E C M T R K.
examples.answer: Postorder A E C M T R K. The first item of preorder gives the root; its position in the inorder splits left from right.

examples.setup: A binary tree has postorder D F E B G C A and inorder D B F E A G C. Rebuild it, then give the preorder and the height (in edges).
steps: In postorder the root is last: A. Inorder: D B F E | A | G C. Left subtree has 4 nodes, right has 2.
Left postorder is the first 4 items, D F E B: the root is B. Inorder D | B | F E: left child D, and the right part is F E.
For the right part, postorder is F E, so its root is E. Inorder F | E: F is the left child of E.
Right subtree of A: postorder G C, so the root is C. Inorder G | C: G is the left child of C.
The tree is A(B(D, E(F, -)), C(G, -)). Preorder: A B D E F C G. The longest path A, B, E, F has 3 edges.
examples.answer: Preorder A B D E F C G and height 3. Postorder works like preorder from the other end: the last item is the root.

examples.setup: A node A has exactly one child, B. Preorder is A B and postorder is B A. Is the tree determined by these two sequences?
steps: If B is the left child of A: preorder A B, postorder B A.
If B is the right child of A: preorder A B, postorder B A. The same two sequences.
The two traversals cannot tell which side B hangs on.
With inorder you could: B A means B is on the left, A B means B is on the right.
examples.answer: Not determined. Preorder with postorder identifies a tree only if every node has 0 or 2 children (a full binary tree). Inorder together with either of the others always works.

edge_cases: Pre + post: unique only for full binary trees.
Pre + in or post + in: always unique (distinct labels).
A node with no left part in the inorder has no left child.
Duplicate labels make rebuilding ambiguous.

cards.title: BST property, search and insert
cards.simple: A BST is a tree for playing 'higher or lower'. At each node you ask whether your key is smaller or larger than the one you see. Smaller means go left and larger means go right. When you reach an empty spot, that is where the key lives or where it should be added. The same walk is used for searching and for inserting. The speed depends on how many steps down you go, which is the height of the tree. In exam words: BST property is left keys < node < right keys for the whole subtree; search and insert follow one path and cost O(height).
cards.idea: A **binary search tree** keeps its keys ordered so that you can discard half of the tree at every step. For every node, all keys in its left subtree are smaller, and all keys in its right subtree are larger. Search and insert both walk down one path from the root.
cards.definition:
BST property: for every node `x`, every key in the left subtree of `x` is `< x.key`, and every key in the right subtree is `> x.key`.

- **Search(k):** start at the root; if `k` equals the node, found; if smaller, go left; if larger, go right; an empty slot means not found.
- **Insert(k):** do the same walk; place the new node at the empty slot where it ended.
- Cost: the number of nodes on the path, at most `height + 1`, so `O(height)`.
cards.intuition_full: Each comparison tells you which side the key must be in, because the property covers the entire subtree and not only the children. So the other side can be thrown away, just as in binary search on a sorted array. Insertion puts the new key where a search for it would have ended, so a later search finds it. The tree's shape is created by the insertion order, which is why the cost can vary from log n to n. The property is a statement about whole subtrees: a node with a smaller left child and a larger right child can still sit in the wrong place if a deeper key breaks the rule. A reliable test is the inorder traversal: a tree is a BST exactly when its inorder is strictly increasing.

examples.setup: Insert the keys 40, 20, 60, 10, 30, 50, 35 in this order into an empty BST, then search for 35. How many nodes does the search compare and how many edges does it follow?
steps: Insert 40: it becomes the root. Insert 20: 20 < 40, so go left. Insert 60: 60 > 40, so go right.
Insert 10: 10 < 40, go left to 20; 10 < 20, go left. Insert 30: left at 40, then 30 > 20, so right of 20.
Insert 50: 50 > 40, go right to 60; 50 < 60, so left of 60.
Insert 35: at 40 go left (35 < 40); at 20 go right (35 > 20); at 30 go right (35 > 30). The slot is empty, so 35 is the right child of 30.
Search 35 follows the same path: 40, 20, 30, 35. That compares 4 nodes and follows 3 edges.
examples.answer: The search compares 4 nodes and follows 3 edges. Search and insert use the same path; the path length is at most the height.

examples.setup: The keys 38, 21, 52, 12, 30, 45, 61, 27, 33 are inserted in this order into an empty BST. How many edges are on the path from the root to 33, and how many key comparisons does an unsuccessful search for 29 make?
steps: Build: 38 is the root. 21 goes left, 52 right. 12 goes left of 21. 30 is under 21 on the right. 45 and 61 go under 52.
27: 38 -> left to 21 -> right to 30 -> left of 30. 33: 38 -> 21 -> 30 -> right of 30.
Path to 33: 38, 21, 30, 33. That is 3 edges.
Search for 29: compare with 38 (go left), 21 (go right), 30 (go left), 27 (go right). Right of 27 is empty. That is 4 comparisons, then it stops with 'not found'.
examples.answer: 3 edges to reach 33 and 4 comparisons for the unsuccessful search for 29. An unsuccessful search ends at an empty slot after comparing every node on the path.

examples.setup: A binary tree has root 10, left child 5, and 5's right child 15; 10's right child is 20. Every node is larger than its left child and smaller than its right child. Is it a BST?
steps: Check each node against its children: 5 < 10 (left of 10), 20 > 10 (right of 10), 15 > 5 (right of 5).
Every parent-child pair looks fine.
But 15 lies in the **left subtree of 10**, and the BST rule says every key in the left subtree must be smaller than 10. 15 > 10.
So the tree is not a BST: the rule applies to the whole subtree, not just to direct children.
examples.answer: Not a BST. Checking only parent and child is not enough; each key must fit within the bounds set by all its ancestors. Inorder gives 5 15 10 20, which is not sorted.

Search miss ends at an empty slot after comparing every node on the path.

cards.title: BST traversals
cards.simple: If you read the keys of a BST from left to right, you get them in sorted order, like books on a shelf. That reading is the inorder traversal. The preorder lists every node before its children, and that is also an order in which the keys could have been added. So adding the keys one by one in preorder rebuilds the same tree. One list of keys is enough, because the sorted order is already known. In exam words: the inorder of a BST is the sorted key list; a BST can be rebuilt from its preorder alone, or from its postorder alone, because the inorder is known.
cards.idea: A BST makes its **inorder** traversal sorted: left keys are smaller, so they come first. That means a BST is fixed by its key set plus either its preorder or its postorder, with no second traversal needed. Rebuilding is repeated insertion, or splitting at the first larger key.
cards.definition:
- **Inorder of a BST** = the keys in increasing order.
- **From preorder:** insert the keys in the given order, or: the first key is the root, the keys up to the first larger key form the left subtree, the rest form the right subtree.
- **From postorder:** the last key is the root; the keys before it split into the smaller ones (left subtree) and larger ones (right subtree), taken in order.
- A tree is a BST exactly when its inorder is strictly increasing.
cards.intuition_full: Inorder is sorted because of the BST rule itself: everything in the left subtree is smaller than the node, and everything in the right subtree is larger, so 'left subtree, node, right subtree' is increasing at every level. The preorder then gives the shape: the root is first, and since smaller keys must go left, the first key greater than the root marks where the right subtree begins. In postorder the root is last and the same split works from the other end. The sorted inorder is the missing second sequence that made the general rebuild in the previous card possible. That also explains why traversals of an arbitrary binary tree are less informative: with no ordering there is nothing to split on. As a test for an unknown tree, compute the inorder and see if it increases.

examples.setup: The preorder traversal of a BST is 45, 20, 10, 30, 25, 60, 50, 70. Rebuild the BST and write its inorder and postorder.
steps: Preorder lists a node before its subtrees, so inserting the keys in this order rebuilds the same BST. Insert 45 (root), 20 (left of 45), 10 (left of 20), 30 (right of 20), 25 (left of 30).
Insert 60 (right of 45), 50 (left of 60), 70 (right of 60). The tree is 45(20(10, 30(25, -)), 60(50, 70)).
Inorder of a BST is always sorted: 10 20 25 30 45 50 60 70.
Postorder (left, right, node): 10 25 30 20, then 50 70 60, then the root 45.
examples.answer: Inorder 10 20 25 30 45 50 60 70; postorder 10 25 30 20 50 70 60 45. No second traversal was needed, because a BST's inorder is the sorted keys.

examples.setup: The postorder traversal of a BST is 3, 7, 5, 4, 12, 20, 15, 11. What is its preorder traversal?
steps: In postorder the root is last: 11. The keys before it are the left subtree (all < 11) and then the right subtree (all > 11): 3 7 5 4 | 12 20 15.
Left group 3 7 5 4: its root is its last key, 4. Smaller keys: 3. Larger keys: 7 5. In the group 7 5 the root is 5, and 7 > 5 goes to its right.
Right group 12 20 15: its root is 15. Smaller: 12. Larger: 20.
The tree is 11(4(3, 5(-, 7)), 15(12, 20)). Preorder (node, left, right): 11 4 3 5 7 15 12 20.
examples.answer: Preorder 11 4 3 5 7 15 12 20. For a BST the inorder is known (the sorted keys), so the pair (postorder, sorted keys) rebuilds the tree.

examples.setup: The preorder of a BST is 3, 1, 2. Is the tree unique? What if the labels A, B, C are not keys and the tree is any binary tree?
steps: Insert 3 (root), then 1: 1 < 3, left of 3. Then 2: 2 < 3, go left to 1; 2 > 1, so right of 1. Tree 3(1(-, 2), -).
Could another BST have preorder 3 1 2? After the root 3, the next key 1 must be its left child (1 < 3). Then 2 < 3 puts it in the left subtree, and 2 > 1 makes it 1's right child. Only one tree.
A general binary tree with preorder A B C has no key order to guide it. The five shapes are: A(B(C, -), -), A(B(-, C), -), A(B, C), A(-, B(C, -)), A(-, B(-, C)).
So the key ordering is what lets a single traversal rebuild a BST.
examples.answer: Unique for the BST (one tree), but five different binary trees fit preorder A B C. The BST property replaces the missing inorder.

Rebuild: first key of preorder (or last of postorder) is the root.
Split the remaining keys into smaller and larger than the root.
Recurse on both groups, then read off the traversal you need.
cards.mistake: Splitting at the wrong place, for example at the middle of the sequence. The split is at the first key larger than the root (in preorder), and the left and right parts need not have equal size. Another slip is reading postorder from the left, where the root is at the end.
edge_cases: Preorder of a BST that is a right chain is sorted.
All keys smaller than the root: the right subtree is empty.
Strictly increasing inorder rules out duplicates.
Only the BST property makes one traversal enough.

cards.what_full:
A BST makes its **inorder** traversal sorted: left keys are smaller, so they come first. That means a BST is fixed by its key set plus either its preorder or its postorder, with no second traversal needed. Rebuilding is repeated insertion, or splitting at the first larger key.

- **Inorder of a BST** = the keys in increasing order.
- **From preorder:** insert the keys in the given order, or: the first key is the root, the keys up to the first larger key form the left subtree, the rest form the right subtree.
- **From postorder:** the last key is the root; the keys before it split into the smaller ones (left subtree) and larger ones (right subtree), taken in order.
- A tree is a BST exactly when its inorder is strictly increasing.

**Worked example.** The preorder traversal of a BST is 45, 20, 10, 30, 25, 60, 50, 70. Rebuild the BST and write its inorder and postorder.

1. Preorder lists a node before its subtrees, so inserting the keys in this order rebuilds the same BST. Insert 45 (root), 20 (left of 45), 10 (left of 20), 30 (right of 20), 25 (left of 30).
2. Insert 60 (right of 45), 50 (left of 60), 70 (right of 60). The tree is 45(20(10, 30(25, -)), 60(50, 70)).
3. Inorder of a BST is always sorted: 10 20 25 30 45 50 60 70.
4. Postorder (left, right, node): 10 25 30 20, then 50 70 60, then the root 45.

cards.title: BST deletion
cards.simple: Deleting from a BST is like removing a person from a sorted line without leaving a gap. If nobody hangs off them, just take them out. If they have one child, that child steps up into their place. If they have two, you need a replacement who keeps the order: the next-larger key, which is the smallest one on the right. Copy that key into the spot, then remove the replacement from where it was. In exam words: delete a leaf by removing it, a one-child node by bypassing it, and a two-child node by copying its inorder successor and then deleting that successor.
cards.idea: Deleting a key from a BST must keep the BST property. There are three cases, by the number of children of the node to delete: none, one, or two. The two-child case uses the **inorder successor** (the smallest key in the right subtree) or the **predecessor** (the largest key in the left subtree).
cards.definition:
To delete node `x`:

- **No children:** remove `x`.
- **One child:** replace `x` by its child (bypass).
- **Two children:** find `s`, the inorder successor (go right once, then left as far as possible). Copy `s.key` into `x`, then delete `s` from the right subtree. `s` has no left child, so this is the easy case.

Cost: `O(height)`.
cards.intuition_full: The successor is the right choice because it is the only key that can take the place of x without breaking the order. It is larger than everything in the left subtree (it is in the right subtree of x), and it is smaller than everything else in the right subtree (it is the minimum there). So the left subtree and the rest of the right subtree remain correctly on either side. The successor has no left child by definition, because the walk went left until it could not, so removing it falls into the easy cases (leaf, or one right child). The predecessor does the mirror job and is equally correct, and it can give a different tree shape. Questions always say which rule to use. Notice that you copy a key, then delete a node, and the node deleted is not the one you started with. Forgetting the second step leaves a duplicate.

examples.setup: In the BST built by inserting 55, 30, 75, 20, 45, 65, 85, 40, 50, delete the key 30 using the inorder successor.
steps: Node 30 has two children (20 and 45), so it cannot be removed directly.
The inorder successor is the smallest key in the right subtree. Go right to 45, then left as far as possible: 40 (40 has no left child).
Copy 40 into the node that held 30. Now the tree holds 40 twice.
Delete the original 40 from the right subtree. It is a leaf, so it is removed.
The tree is 55(40(20, 45(-, 50)), 75(65, 85)). Its inorder is 20 40 45 50 55 65 75 85, still sorted.
examples.answer: 30 is replaced by its successor 40. The preorder afterwards is 55 40 20 45 50 75 65 85.

examples.setup: Start with the BST built by inserting 60, 40, 90, 25, 50, 70, 100, 65. Delete 70, then delete 60 (the root) using the inorder successor. Give the preorder of the final tree.
steps: Delete 70: it has one child, 65. Bypass 70 so that 90's left child becomes 65.
Delete 60 (two children). Its successor is the smallest key in the right subtree: go right to 90, then left to 65. 65 has no left child, so the successor is 65.
Copy 65 into the root. Delete the old 65 node: it is a leaf, the left child of 90, so remove it.
examples.answer: Preorder 65 40 25 50 90 100. A leaf is removed, a one-child node is bypassed, and a two-child node takes its successor's key.

examples.setup: In the BST 50(30, 70(60, 80)), a programmer deletes 50 with the successor rule but forgets the last step, removing the old successor node. What does the tree look like, and what is the correct tree?
steps: Node 50 has two children. The successor is the smallest key in the right subtree: go right to 70, then left to 60.
Copy 60 into the root. The root now holds 60.
Bug: the old node 60 stays as 70's left child. The inorder becomes 30 60 60 70 80: the key 60 appears twice and the tree still has 5 nodes.
Correct: also remove the old 60 (a leaf). The tree is 60(30, 70(-, 80)) with inorder 30 60 70 80.
examples.answer: The buggy tree holds 60 twice; the correct tree is 60(30, 70(-, 80)). The predecessor rule would use 30 instead; both are valid, and the question says which.

cards.title: BST shape and insertion order
cards.simple: The same set of keys can build a tall thin tree or a short bushy one, depending only on the order you add them. Add keys already in order and you get a staircase: every search walks the whole way down. Add the middle key first, then the middles of each half, and you get a short, wide tree. Same keys, same sorted reading, very different speed. In exam words: BST height ranges from floor(log2 n) to n - 1, and the insertion order decides the shape.
cards.idea: A BST has no rule about shape, only about order. The first key becomes the root, and every later key goes where a search for it ends. So each different insertion order can give a different tree. The height can be as small as floor(log2 n) or as large as n - 1.
cards.definition:
For `n` distinct keys inserted into an empty BST:

- **Minimum height:** `floor(log2 n)`, reached by the (almost) perfect tree.
- **Maximum height:** `n - 1`, a chain; it occurs when each key is the smallest or the largest of those still to come.
- Number of insertion orders giving a height `n - 1` tree: `2^(n-1)`.
- Inorder is always the sorted keys, whatever the order.
cards.intuition_full: The root is the first key, so it splits the remaining keys into those that go left and those that go right. A good first key (the median) splits evenly; a bad one (the minimum or maximum) leaves everything on one side, and the same thing happens at every level of the chain. Thinking recursively, the shape of a BST is decided by a series of 'who is first among my subtree's keys' choices. This also tells you what the insertion orders for a fixed tree look like: each parent before its children, with the two subtrees free to interleave. The number of such orders is the number of linear arrangements respecting that parent-before-child rule. Zigzag orders such as 1, n, 2, n-1, ... still give a chain, because each new key is the minimum or the maximum of the keys still missing.

examples.setup: Build a BST from the keys 1 to 7 in two ways: inserted in the order 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and in the order 4, 2, 6, 1, 3, 5, 7. Compare the heights and the cost of searching for 7.
steps: Order 1, 2, ..., 7: each key is larger than everything before it, so it goes to the right of the last node. The tree is a chain.
The chain has height 6 (7 nodes, 6 edges). Searching for 7 compares 1, 2, ..., 7: 7 comparisons, O(n).
Order 4, 2, 6, 1, 3, 5, 7: 4 is the root, 2 and 6 hang under it, and 1, 3, 5, 7 fill the last level. The tree is perfect.
Height 2 = floor(log2 7). Searching for 7 compares 4, 6, 7: 3 comparisons. Both trees have the same inorder, 1 to 7.
examples.answer: Chain: height 6 and 7 comparisons. Perfect tree: height 2 and 3 comparisons. The insertion order alone decides the shape.

examples.setup: In how many different insertion orders of the keys 1 to 7 does the BST come out as the perfect tree with root 4, children 2 and 6, and leaves 1, 3, 5, 7?
steps: Every key must be inserted after its parent. So 4 comes first.
After 4, the left part {2, 1, 3} and the right part {6, 5, 7} are independent. Inside each part the middle key (2 or 6) must come before its two leaves.
Each part has 2 valid internal orders: the root first, then the two leaves in either order (2, 1, 3 or 2, 3, 1).
The two sequences of 3 keys can be interleaved in C(6, 3) = 20 ways.
Total = 20 x 2 x 2 = 80.
examples.answer: 80 orders (checked by trying all 5040 permutations). Counting orders = interleavings of the independent subtrees, with each parent before its children.

examples.setup: Insert the keys 1, 7, 2, 6, 3, 5, 4 in this order. The order is not sorted. What is the height of the tree?
steps: Insert 1: root. Insert 7: right of 1.
Insert 2: 2 > 1 go right to 7; 2 < 7, left of 7. Insert 6: right at 1, left at 7, then 6 > 2: right of 2.
Insert 3: ... down to 6, then 3 < 6: left of 6. Insert 5: down to 3, then 5 > 3: right of 3. Insert 4: down to 5, then 4 < 5: left of 5.
Every node has exactly one child, zigzagging right, left, right, left, right, left. 7 nodes in a path: height 6.
examples.answer: Height 6, the same as the sorted chain. Alternating small and large keys also produces a path, so 'not sorted' does not mean 'balanced'.

cards.title: Counting trees
cards.simple: How many different tree shapes can you make with n nodes? Pick which key is the root, say the 3rd of 6. Then the 2 smaller keys form the left subtree and the 3 larger form the right, and you can choose those two shapes independently, so you multiply. Add up over every choice of root. The numbers that come out are 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, and so on. In exam words: the number of binary tree shapes (and of BSTs) on n keys is the Catalan number C(2n, n)/(n + 1): 5 for n = 3 and 14 for n = 4.
cards.idea: The number of different BSTs on `n` distinct keys is the same as the number of binary tree shapes with `n` nodes: the **Catalan number** `C_n`. You can count them by choosing the root and multiplying the counts of the two subtrees.
cards.definition:
Let `C_n` be the number of binary tree shapes (or BSTs) with `n` nodes.

- `C_0 = 1` and `C_n = C_0 x C_(n-1) + C_1 x C_(n-2) + ... + C_(n-1) x C_0`.
- Closed form: `C_n = (1 / (n + 1)) x (2n choose n)`.
- Values: `C_0..C_7 = 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132, 429`.
- BSTs with a given root `r` among `n` keys: `C_(r-1) x C_(n-r)`.
cards.intuition_full: The recurrence comes straight from the structure of a tree: a tree is a root with a left tree and a right tree, so the size of the left tree can be anything from 0 to n-1 and the right takes the rest. Each split gives C_left times C_right shapes, because the two sides are chosen independently. Summing over all splits gives the formula. For BSTs the keys do not add freedom, since once the shape is fixed the keys are forced into the sorted inorder positions. For labelled trees with no order rule, you must multiply by the number of ways to place labels, which is n!. The same Catalan numbers count stack permutations, balanced bracket strings and the ways to parenthesise a product, which is why they show up so often.

examples.setup: How many structurally different BSTs can be built on the keys 1, 2, 3, 4?
steps: Count by the choice of root. If the root is key r, the smaller keys form the left subtree and the larger keys form the right subtree.
Root 1: left is empty (1 way), right holds {2, 3, 4} (C3 = 5 ways). Total 1 x 5 = 5.
Root 2: left {1} (1 way), right {3, 4} (C2 = 2 ways). Total 1 x 2 = 2.
Root 3: left {1, 2} (2 ways), right {4} (1 way). Total 2 x 1 = 2.
Root 4: left {1, 2, 3} (5 ways), right empty. Total 5.
examples.answer: 14 BSTs. The sequence of counts for n = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 is 1, 1, 2, 5, 14: the Catalan numbers.

examples.setup: How many BSTs on the keys 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 have 3 as the root? And how many BSTs are there on 7 keys in all?
steps: Root 3: the smaller keys {1, 2} form the left subtree. The larger keys {4, 5, 6, 7} form the right subtree.
Left: C2 = 2 shapes. Right: C4 = 14 shapes.
The two choices are independent, so they multiply: 2 x 14 = 28.
For all 7 keys, sum over every root: C7 = C(14, 7) / 8 = 3432 / 8 = 429.
examples.answer: 28 BSTs have root 3, out of 429 in total. Counting trees by root turns the problem into a product of smaller Catalan numbers.

examples.setup: How many different binary trees with 3 distinct labelled nodes A, B, C are there if there is no ordering rule? And how many of them are BSTs for the keys 1, 2, 3?
steps: There are C3 = 5 shapes of a binary tree with 3 nodes.
With labels A, B, C and no rule, each shape can be labelled in 3! = 6 ways, and each labelling is a different tree.
So the total is 5 x 6 = 30 labelled trees.
For a BST, the inorder must be sorted. That fixes the labelling of each shape, so there is exactly 1 BST per shape: 5.
examples.answer: 30 labelled binary trees, but only 5 BSTs. The ordering rule leaves one labelling per shape.

cards.title: AVL trees
cards.simple: A tree that grows lopsided gets slow. An AVL tree keeps itself tidy. After every insertion it checks the ancestors of the new node, and if one side has become two levels taller than the other, it twists a few links (a rotation) to even them out, like restacking a leaning pile of books. The twist never changes the sorted order. Because the two sides never differ by more than one level, the height stays small. In exam words: an AVL tree keeps balance factors in {-1, 0, 1} using single or double rotations; its height is O(log n) and the fewest nodes for height h is N(h) = N(h-1) + N(h-2) + 1.
cards.idea: An **AVL tree** is a BST in which, for every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. After an insertion or deletion breaks this, **rotations** restore it. Rotations only rearrange a few pointers and keep the inorder unchanged.
cards.definition:
- **Balance factor** `BF(x) = height(left) - height(right)`. AVL requires `BF in {-1, 0, 1}` at every node.
- **Four cases** at the lowest unbalanced node `z` after an insertion: left-left (one right rotation), right-right (one left rotation), left-right (left rotation at the child, then right rotation at `z`), right-left (the mirror).
- **Minimum nodes** of height `h`: `N(h) = N(h-1) + N(h-2) + 1`, `N(0) = 1`, `N(1) = 2`.
- Height is at most about `1.44 log2 n`, so search, insert, delete are `O(log n)`.
cards.intuition_full: Two things need explaining: why rotations work, and why the height stays logarithmic. A rotation lifts a middle key above its neighbours while keeping left-to-right order: 10 < 20 < 30 stays in that order whether 10, 20 or 30 is on top. So it changes the shape, never the inorder. Choosing the rotation depends on which way the heavy side bends. If the heavy child leans the same way (left-left), one rotation in the opposite direction is enough. If it leans the other way (left-right), the child must first be turned so that the lean is straight, then rotated as before. As for height: the sparsest AVL tree of height h hangs a sparsest tree of height h-1 and one of height h-2 under a root. That gives N(h), which grows like the Fibonacci numbers, exponentially in h. So n nodes force h to be at most proportional to log n. After an insertion only the lowest unbalanced ancestor needs fixing, since the fix restores the subtree to its earlier height.

examples.setup: Insert 30, then 10, then 20 into an empty AVL tree. What happens at the third insertion, and what is the final tree?
steps: Insert 30: the root. Insert 10: 10 < 30, left of 30. The tree 30(10, -) is still balanced (balance factor of 30 is +1).
Insert 20: 20 < 30, go left to 10; 20 > 10, right of 10. The tree is 30(10(-, 20), -).
Balance factor of 30 = height(left) - height(right) = 2 - 0 = +2. It is outside {-1, 0, 1}, so we must rotate. The left child 10 leans right (BF -1): the left-right (LR) case.
First a left rotation at 10: 20 moves up, so the tree becomes 30(20(10, -), -).
Then a right rotation at 30: 20 becomes the root with children 10 and 30. All balance factors are 0.
examples.answer: The third insertion causes a left-right double rotation (two rotations). The final tree is 20(10, 30).

examples.setup: What is the largest possible height (in edges) of an AVL tree with 40 nodes?
steps: Let N(h) be the fewest nodes an AVL tree of height h can have. The sparsest tree has one subtree of height h - 1 and the other of height h - 2.
40 nodes: N(6) = 33 <= 40 < N(7) = 54. So the height can be at most 6 (and at least floor(log2 40) = 5).

examples.setup: Insert 2, 1, 3, 4, 5 into an empty AVL tree. Several nodes may look unbalanced after inserting 5. Which rotation fixes the tree, and how many rotations are needed?
steps: Insert 2, 1, 3: the tree 2(1, 3) is perfect. Insert 4: right of 3. Tree 2(1, 3(-, 4)). Balance factors are fine (BF of 2 is -1).
Insert 5: right of 4. Now node 3 has BF -2 (right-right) and node 2 also has BF -2 (left height 0, right height 2).
Fix the lowest unbalanced node on the path from the new key: node 3. Right-right case: one left rotation at 3. Node 4 moves up, with children 3 and 5.
The tree is 2(1, 4(3, 5)). Node 2 now has BF 0 - 1 = -1, which is allowed. No further rotation is needed.
examples.answer: One left rotation at node 3. Fixing the lowest unbalanced ancestor restores the height of its subtree, so the ancestors above are fixed as well.

cards.title: Complete tree in an array
cards.simple: A complete tree has no gaps except at the end of the last row, so you can write it into an array row by row, like reading a table. No pointers are needed. Counting from 0, the children of the box at position i sit at positions 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and its parent sits at (i - 1) / 2 rounded down. It is arithmetic on positions. In exam words: array form of a complete binary tree, 0-based: children 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, parent floor((i - 1) / 2); 1-based: children 2i and 2i + 1, parent floor(i / 2).
cards.idea: A complete binary tree fills every level from the top, and fills the last level from the left. Because there are no gaps, you can store its nodes in an array in level order and find any relative by arithmetic. This is how heaps are stored.
cards.definition:
Array `A` holds a complete binary tree with `n` nodes in level order.

- **0-based:** children of `i` are `2i + 1` and `2i + 2`; parent is `floor((i - 1) / 2)`.
- **1-based:** children of `i` are `2i` and `2i + 1`; parent is `floor(i / 2)`.
- Node `i` is a leaf if its left child index is `>= n` (0-based) or `> n` (1-based).
- Number of leaves: `n - floor(n / 2)`. Height: `floor(log2 n)`.
cards.intuition_full: The formulas follow from counting. In a perfect tree, level k has 2^k nodes, and the nodes before level k number 2^k - 1. The node at position j in level k has index 2^k - 1 + j, and its children are the nodes at positions 2j and 2j + 1 of level k + 1, with indices 2^(k+1) - 1 + 2j and 2^(k+1) + 2j. Subtracting gives 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. The completeness condition guarantees that the array has no holes, so this index arithmetic always lands on a real node when the index is less than n. A tree that is not complete would need placeholder cells for the missing nodes, and the worst case is exponential waste, as the chain example shows. That is why array form is reserved for complete trees such as heaps, and why the arithmetic is worth memorising in both 0-based and 1-based forms.

examples.setup: A complete binary tree is stored level by level in the 0-based array [50, 30, 40, 10, 25, 35, 45, 5, 8]. Find the children of index 1 and index 3, and the parent of index 7 with its value.
steps: Level order is stored left to right, top to bottom. Index 0 is the root: 50.
The children of index `i` are `2i + 1` and `2i + 2`. For i = 0 they are indices 1 and 2 (values 30 and 40).
For i = 1 the children are 3 and 4 (values 10 and 25). For i = 2 they are 5 and 6 (values 35 and 45).
For i = 3 the children are 7 and 8 (values 5 and 8). Index 4 would have children 9 and 10, but only 9 items are stored, so indices 4 to 8 are leaves.
The parent of index 7 is `floor((7 - 1) / 2) = 3`, which holds the value 10.
examples.answer: Children of index 1: indices 3 and 4 (10 and 25). Children of index 3: indices 7 and 8 (5 and 8). Parent of index 7: index 3, value 10.

examples.setup: A complete binary tree with n = 20 nodes is stored in an array with 1-based indexing (root at index 1, children of i at 2i and 2i + 1). How many leaves does it have, what is the index of the last internal node, what is its height in edges, and what is the parent of the node at index 17?
steps: A node i has a child only if its left child 2i is at most n. So internal nodes satisfy 2i <= 20, that is i <= 10.
Indices 1 to 10 are internal and 11 to 20 are leaves: 10 leaves, and the last internal node is at index 10.
Level k occupies indices 2^k to 2^(k+1) - 1. Index 20 lies in 16 to 31, which is level 4, so the height is 4.
The parent of index 17 is floor(17 / 2) = 8.
examples.answer: 10 leaves, last internal node at index 10, height 4, parent of 17 is 8. A complete tree has n - floor(n/2) leaves and height floor(log2 n).

examples.setup: A binary tree with 5 nodes is a chain in which every node is the right child of its parent. It is stored in an array with 1-based indexing (right child of i at 2i + 1). How large must the array be?
steps: The root is at index 1.
Its right child is at 2 x 1 + 1 = 3. That node's right child is at 2 x 3 + 1 = 7.
The five nodes sit at indices 1, 3, 7, 15, 31. The array must have at least 31 cells and 26 stay empty.

cards.title: Operation costs
cards.simple: How long does a BST take? Each search, insert or delete walks down a single path from the root, and the path is at most as long as the height of the tree. A balanced tree with a million keys has a height of about 20, so about 20 steps. A lopsided one could need a million. To list all keys between two values, first walk down to the start, then collect the next k keys in order. In exam words: BST search, insert and delete cost O(height); on a balanced BST that is O(log n), and a range query costs O(log n + k).
cards.idea: BST operations move down one path, so their cost is the height of the tree, not the number of nodes. Whether that is good depends on the shape. Balanced trees keep the height at O(log n); an unbalanced tree can degrade to O(n). A range query finds the start in O(height) and then reports k keys.
cards.definition:
For a BST with height `h` and `n` nodes:

- **Search, insert, delete:** `O(h)`; worst case `O(n)`, balanced `O(log n)`.
- **Minimum / maximum:** follow left (or right) pointers, `O(h)`.
- **Range query** reporting `k` keys: `O(h + k)`, which is `O(log n + k)` when balanced.
- **Building** a BST by `n` insertions: sum of path lengths; `O(n log n)` expected for random order, `Theta(n^2)` for sorted input.
cards.intuition_full: Everything follows from the fact that each step discards a subtree. After a comparison you commit to one child, so the work is the length of one root-to-node path. That length is bounded by the height, which is why the height appears in every bound. A range query adds a second term because it must also visit the keys it reports: finding the first key in range costs a root-to-node walk, and then successive keys in inorder order are reached by moving to the next key, which in total touches only the nodes on the walk and the k reported keys (plus the ancestors on the way back). The cost of building a BST is the sum of the depths at which nodes are inserted. For a chain this sum is 0 + 1 + ... + (n - 1), quadratic, and for a balanced tree each insertion costs about log n.

examples.setup: Report all keys in the range [25, 55] from the BST 40(20(10, 30), 60(50, 70)). Which nodes are examined, and why is the cost O(log n + k)?
steps: The tree is 40 with children 20 and 60. 20 has children 10 and 30; 60 has children 50 and 70. The range is [25, 55].
Find where 25 would be: at 40 go left (25 < 40); at 20 go right (25 > 20); at 30, which is >= 25, the first key in the range.
Report 30.
Continue in inorder order. The next key is 40, in range: report it. Then 50 (the left child of 60), in range: report it.
The next key is 60 > 55, so stop. The reported keys are 30, 40, 50, so k = 3. Only 5 of the 7 nodes were examined; 10 and 70 were never visited.
examples.answer: Reported 30, 40, 50 using one walk of length about the height plus k reported keys: O(log n + k) on a balanced tree.

steps: Inserting key k into the chain of the k - 1 keys already present compares it with all of them: k - 1 comparisons (k > every key, so it goes right each time).
The comparison counts are 0, 1, 2, ..., 9.
A balanced tree would use about log2 k comparisons per insertion, for a total of O(n log n).
examples.answer: 45 comparisons. Sorted insertion into an unbalanced BST costs Theta(n^2) in total because the tree is a chain of height n - 1.

examples.setup: In the BST that is a right chain 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 (each node is the right child of the previous), how many nodes does it take to find the minimum, and to find the maximum?
steps: Minimum: start at the root and go left as long as there is a left child. The root, 1, has none, so the minimum is found at once: 1 node visited.
Maximum: start at the root and go right until there is no right child: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. That visits 5 nodes.
Both costs are bounded by the height (4 edges here), but the actual cost depends on the shape and on which key is wanted.
A chain makes one end cheap and the other expensive.
examples.answer: 1 node for the minimum and 5 for the maximum. Costs are O(height) as an upper bound; the shape decides each case.

cards.title: Recursion on trees
cards.simple: To answer a question about a whole tree, ask a helper to answer it for the left side and another helper for the right side, and then combine their answers with the root. An empty side is the easiest case and answers straight away. For example, the number of leaves is the leaves on the left plus the leaves on the right. Each helper does exactly the same job on a smaller tree, so the work ends when a helper is handed nothing. cards.idea: A binary tree is a root with two smaller binary trees, so most tree functions are recursive. The base case is the empty tree (NULL). Template:

`f(p)`: if `p == NULL` return `base`; else `l = f(p->left)`, `r = f(p->right)`, return `combine(p->data, l, r)`.

cards.intuition_full: This is the same pattern as for lists, with two recursive calls instead of one. The function trusts that f(left) and f(right) are correct, and only has to say how the root's answer follows from them. That is also how you trace: go down the left spine first, return the leaf answers, then work upward. If the code prints in the middle or at the end of the function body, then the print happens when the call is returning, so the printed order is inorder or postorder. The base case is not only a stopping condition. It sets the unit of the answer, for example height in edges when NULL returns -1. A function that reads p->left or p->right before checking p crashes on an empty tree, so the NULL test comes first.

cards.title: Trees in Python
cards.simple: In Python you can build a tree out of tuples. Each node is a tuple (label, left, right), and an empty side is None. The same recursion as in C works, with `t is None` as the base case. To visit a tree level by level, put the root in a queue, take one out, record it, and put its two children at the back. In exam words: trees in Python are nested tuples or Node objects; recursion with a None check handles depth-first work, and a deque handles level order.
cards.idea: A Python tree is a nested tuple `(label, left, right)` or an object with `val`, `left` and `right` attributes. `None` marks an empty subtree. Depth-first functions use recursion with a `None` check. Level order uses `collections.deque` as the queue.
cards.definition:
- Node: `(label, left, right)`; `t[0]` label, `t[1]` left subtree, `t[2]` right subtree; `None` is empty.
- Recursion: `def f(t): if t is None: return base; return combine(t[0], f(t[1]), f(t[2]))`.
- Level order: `q = deque([root])`; loop: `popleft`, skip `None`, record the label, append both children.
- Tuples are immutable: to 'change' a tree, build new tuples along the path.
cards.intuition_full: The tuple form is a literal copy of the mathematical definition: a tree is a label with two trees, and the empty tree is None. That makes recursive functions short, and the base case `t is None` plays the role of `p == NULL` in C. Indexing needs care: `t[1][2][0]` means 'left subtree, then its right subtree, then its label'. For level order you cannot use recursion directly, because you must finish a row before the next, so you use a first-in, first-out queue of pending nodes. A tree with n nodes has n + 1 None children, so a loop that enqueues None entries will process 2n + 1 items in total; skipping the None entries is a good habit. The immutability of tuples explains why many Python programs prefer small classes for mutable trees.

steps: A node is a tuple `(label, left, right)`, and `None` is an empty subtree. M is the root; its left subtree is K (with left child H) and its right subtree is R (with right child T).
`t[1]` is the left subtree `('K', ('H', None, None), None)`, so `t[1][0]` is `'K'`.
`t[2]` is R's tuple. `t[2][2]` is its right subtree `('T', None, None)`, so `t[2][2][0]` is `'T'`.
`size(t)`: M counts 1, plus size of K's subtree (1 + 1 + 0 = 2), plus size of R's subtree (1 + 0 + 1 = 2). That is 1 + 2 + 2 = 5.
examples.answer: It prints `5 K T`. The base case `t is None` ends the recursion; index 0 is the label, 1 the left subtree and 2 the right subtree.

examples.setup:
What does this function return for the same tree `t`, and how many items does the queue dequeue in total?
```python
from collections import deque
def lvl(t):
    q = deque([t]); out = []
    while q:
        n = q.popleft()
        if n is None:
            continue
        out.append(n[0])
        q.append(n[1]); q.append(n[2])
    return out
```
steps: The queue starts as [M]. Dequeue M, record it, and enqueue its children K and R.
Dequeue K: record it, enqueue H and None. Dequeue R: record it, enqueue None and T.
Dequeue H: record it, enqueue None and None. Dequeue None (skipped), None (skipped), then T: record it, enqueue None and None.
The remaining items are all None and are skipped. The recorded order is M, K, R, H, T. The queue handled 5 nodes plus 6 None entries = 11 dequeues.
examples.answer: It returns `['M', 'K', 'R', 'H', 'T']` (level order) after 11 dequeues. A tree with n nodes has n + 1 empty children, which the queue also sees.

examples.setup: A programmer wants to insert a new left child under H in the tuple tree `t` above by writing `t[1][1][1] = ('X', None, None)`. What happens?
steps: `t[1]` is K's tuple. `t[1][1]` is H's tuple. `t[1][1][1]` is H's left slot.
Assigning to an item of a tuple raises a `TypeError`: tuples cannot be changed.
To change the tree you must rebuild the tuples along the path from the root: new H, then new K, then new root.
Alternatively use a class with `left` and `right` attributes, or lists, which can be modified in place.

scenes.title: Depth, leaves, internal nodes and height

steps.caption: Name the parts of a tree. A is the root. Its children are B and C. B has children D and E, E has the child G, and C has the child F.
Depth is the number of edges from the root. A is 0. B and C are 1. D, E and F are 2. G is 3.

set.text: depth: A 0 | B C 1 | D E F 2 | G 3

steps.caption: Leaves have no children: D, G and F. That is 3 leaves.
Internal nodes have at least one child: A, B, C and E. That is 4 internal nodes, and 4 + 3 = 7 nodes in all.
Height is the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. A, B, E, G has 3 edges (4 nodes). So the height is 3, not 4.

scenes.title: Full binary tree: 6 leaves, 5 internal nodes

steps.caption: Count the leaves and internal nodes. The tree shown is full: every node has 0 or 2 children. It has 6 leaves.
Start from a single node: 1 leaf and 0 internal nodes. Give a leaf two children: that node becomes internal (+1 internal), one leaf is lost and two are gained (+1 leaf net).

set.text: a leaf splits: -1 leaf, +2 leaves, +1 internal

steps.caption: So after every such step, leaves = internal + 1. With 6 leaves there are 5 internal nodes.
Total nodes = leaves + internal = 6 + 5 = 11, which is also 2 x 6 - 1.

scenes.title: Preorder, inorder and postorder of one tree

steps.caption: Walk the tree three ways. The tree: P at the top, Q (with S, T) on the left, R (with U, V) on the right, W below V on the right. The three orders differ only in when the node is written relative to its subtrees.
Preorder (node, left, right): write P first, then the whole left subtree in preorder: Q S T.
Then the right subtree in preorder: R U V W. Preorder = P Q S T R U V W.
Inorder (left, node, right): the whole left subtree first, in inorder: S Q T.
Then P, then the right subtree in inorder: U R V W. Inorder = S Q T P U R V W.
Postorder (left, right, node): the left subtree first, in postorder: S T Q.
Then the right subtree in postorder: U W V R, and the root P last. Postorder = S T Q U W V R P.

scenes.title: Preorder gives the root, inorder splits the sides

steps.caption: Split with the root. The first item of the preorder is the root: K. Find K in the inorder: A C E | K | M R T. So the left subtree has 3 nodes (A, C, E) and the right subtree has 3 (M, R, T).
Left subtree: its preorder is the next 3 items, C A E. The first, C, is its root. In the inorder A C E, C splits A | C | E.
A and E are alone on each side of C, so they are C's left and right children (leaves).
Right subtree: its preorder is R M T. The root is R. In the inorder M R T it splits M | R | T, so M and T are leaves.
The tree is K(C(A, E), R(M, T)). Postorder (left, right, node): A E C M T R K.

scenes.title: Insert along a path, search along the same path

steps.caption: Walk higher or lower. Insert 40: it becomes the root. Insert 20: 20 < 40, so go left. Insert 60: 60 > 40, so go right.
Insert 10: 10 < 40, go left to 20; 10 < 20, go left. Insert 30: left at 40, then 30 > 20, so right of 20.
Insert 50: 50 > 40, go right to 60; 50 < 60, so left of 60.
Insert 35: at 40 go left (35 < 40); at 20 go right (35 > 20); at 30 go right (35 > 30). The slot is empty, so 35 is the right child of 30.

set.text: 35: left at 40, right at 20, right at 30

steps.caption: Search 35 follows the same path: 40, 20, 30, 35. That compares 4 nodes and follows 3 edges.

scenes.title: Rebuild a BST from its preorder, then read the traversals

steps.caption: Insert in preorder. Preorder lists a node before its subtrees, so inserting the keys in this order rebuilds the same BST. Insert 45 (root), 20 (left of 45), 10 (left of 20), 30 (right of 20), 25 (left of 30).
Insert 60 (right of 45), 50 (left of 60), 70 (right of 60). The tree is 45(20(10, 30(25, -)), 60(50, 70)).
Inorder of a BST is always sorted: 10 20 25 30 45 50 60 70.
Postorder (left, right, node): 10 25 30 20, then 50 70 60, then the root 45.

scenes.title: Delete 30: copy the successor 40, then remove it

steps.caption: Replace with the successor. Node 30 has two children (20 and 45), so it cannot be removed directly.
The inorder successor is the smallest key in the right subtree. Go right to 45, then left as far as possible: 40 (40 has no left child).
Copy 40 into the node that held 30. Now the tree holds 40 twice.
Delete the original 40 from the right subtree. It is a leaf, so it is removed.
The tree is 55(40(20, 45(-, 50)), 75(65, 85)). Its inorder is 20 40 45 50 55 65 75 85, still sorted.
Same keys, different order. Order 1, 2, ..., 7: each key is larger than everything before it, so it goes to the right of the last node. The tree is a chain.

set.text: sorted keys: each goes right of the last

steps.caption: The chain has height 6 (7 nodes, 6 edges). Searching for 7 compares 1, 2, ..., 7: 7 comparisons, O(n).
Order 4, 2, 6, 1, 3, 5, 7: 4 is the root, 2 and 6 hang under it, and 1, 3, 5, 7 fill the last level. The tree is perfect.
